English appears only as optional translations of key examples and concepts in A1–A2 grammar classes.

additions.text: Pronouns replace a noun we already know.
She puts it in her bag. She greets her.
Pronoun + verb: lo tengo = I have it.
I have the map: I have it.
I have the photo: I have it.
I look for my books: I look for them.
I see Elena: I see her.
to him · to her · to them
I give Elena a book: I give her a book.
I give the folders to my colleagues.
Can you see me? I’m at the door.
I’ll send you a photo of the entrance.
I have them in my bag.
I send them a photo in the afternoon.
I see her at the office.
One verb form tells you who does the action.
You prepare the book at home.
Luis and Marta work a lot.
Spanish often drops the subject pronoun.
Right now I’m working at home.
I work at home on Mondays.
I read the newspaper every morning.
I hope the class is interesting.
Today we study Spanish at six.
They read the newspaper every day.
A noun phrase: one main noun and extra details.
a new book → some new books
a round table → two round tables
the white house → the white houses
Only determiner, noun and adjective agree.
a house with a garden · a lamp with white light
a table for two · a folder for documents
a very big house with a garden
two comfortable chairs for the living room
a big table → una mesa grande
A very big house with a garden.
A sentence needs a conjugated verb.
Ana and Leo prepare the meeting.
Leo and I prepare the meeting.
Leo doesn’t prepare documents in the morning.
Do you have time this afternoon?
Leo and I prepare the documents.
State with participles, groups with singular agreement, and comparisons.
The group prefers the room on the first floor.
The second room is bigger than the first.
This neighbourhood is less noisy than the centre.
The new chairs are more comfortable than the old ones.
This room is as quiet as the library.
The second book is as interesting as the first.
The first room is quieter than the second.
The chairs are as comfortable as the armchairs.
One sentence can say when, how and where something happens.
I study calmly at home in the morning.
I work calmly at home in the morning.
We walk slowly in the park on Sundays.
I read a book on the train every day.
Keep the subject and the verb together.
On Tuesday afternoon we work together in the library.
We work together in the library on Tuesday afternoon.
A long frame at the start often takes a comma.
Do you prefer tea or coffee?
Do you work at home or in an office?
Shall we meet before or after lunch?
Shall we go on Tuesday or on Wednesday?
The voice rises on the first option and falls on the second.
Don’t put every piece at the start.
I work at home in the morning.
Do you prefer Tuesday or Wednesday?
Tomorrow we meet at the library.
We use the present tense for routines.
Nora opens the shop at nine.
I have lunch with a colleague at one.
On Saturdays I visit my family.
No before the verb; questions with ¿? and rising intonation.
Nora is writing a message to a customer now.
Water boils at a hundred degrees.
Some very common verbs are irregular in the “yo” form.
The ending shows the person, so “yo” is optional.
Do you sell books in English?
I visit my family on Saturdays.
Nora is writing a message now.
Something already happened, but we tell it from the present.
Only haber changes; the participle stays the same.
a time period that includes now
I spoke to the teacher today.
This week we have checked all the photos.
This month I started a design course.
I have visited Mexico three times.
I have already chosen the photos, but I haven’t finished the project yet.
a past action with a present result
Marta has lost the folder, so she can’t send her part.
You look tired. What has happened?
I have never been to Japan.
We have worked a lot this week.
I haven’t written the introduction yet.
We use the preterite for finished actions in a finished time.
Last night I had dinner with Laura.
On Saturday we went to the museum.
hablo = I speak · habló = he/she spoke
Context tells you if “hablamos” is present or past.
Common irregular verbs have a new stem and no written accent.
He came in, said hello and sat down.
First we bought a map and then we visited the market.
In the end we came back on the last bus.
We spent two hours at the museum.
I worked in a hotel for three years.
The trip lasted just one day.
Last Saturday we went to the museum.
We spent two hours at the market.
We use the imperfect to describe the past.
The library was small and had big windows.
In winter it was cold, but there was good light.
It was ten o’clock and I was twelve.
As a child I used to play football in the street.
Every summer we used to travel to the coast.
I didn’t use to drink coffee.
Every Friday we all used to eat together.
I was cooking when you called.
While I was looking for a book, I found a note.
I was reading and my classmate was working at the next table.
Every Sunday I used to go to the park.
We use the simple future for predictions.
Tomorrow it will rain all over the country.
I think meetings will be shorter.
In the future we will work fewer hours.
There will probably be some questions.
All forms have an accent except “nosotros”.
Some verbs change the stem but keep the same endings.
I’ll send the address on Friday.
I promise I won’t be late.
If we leave at eight, we’ll arrive on time.
If we share information, we’ll work better.
Present after “si”, future in the result.
There will be a room for calls in the new office.
If you practise every day, you’ll improve.
We use the imperative to give instructions and make requests.
Write a message to the group.
Don’t eat in the room, please.
Don’t use the big room, because there’s a meeting.
Can you close the door, please?
Pronouns attach to affirmative commands and go before negative ones.
habla / no hables · come / no comas
Four small words to connect ideas: and, or, but, nor.
I work from home and study Spanish.
Pablo buys vegetables and Julia sets the table.
The class is practical and fun.
I have a brother and a sister.
y becomes e before an «i» sound.
Shall we cook at your place or go to a café?
Do you want coffee or tea?
We can watch a film or go for a walk.
I arrive at seven or eight.
The café is comfortable, but it is far away.
Julia has pasta, but she has no vegetables.
The apartment is small, but it is comfortable.
The restaurant is expensive, but the food is excellent.
I eat neither meat nor fish.
Julia has no tomatoes or onions.
I drink neither coffee nor tea.
We cook or we go to a café.
The hotel is expensive, but it is nice.
I buy the bread and you set the table.
An opinion, a reason and a goal.
I think the library is a good place.
I think this neighbourhood is quiet.
Leo thinks the café is better.
I study at the library because my house is noisy.
I study Spanish because I travel a lot.
I don’t go to the café because there are lots of people.
I like this neighbourhood because it is quiet.
I go early to prepare my questions.
I go to the market to buy fruit.
I take my notebook to write down new words.
Leo comes to practise Spanish with me.
I think the neighbourhood is quiet.
I study at the library because it is quiet.
Before, after and when: three ways to order a routine.
Before opening my email, I check my to-do list.
I brush my teeth before going to sleep.
Before lunch, I check what I have finished.
After making a coffee, I start with the urgent document.
After lunch, I go for a short walk.
After work, I go to the gym.
When she gets a question, Silvia saves it in a folder.
When I get home, I check my email.
When I have lots of tasks, I take a short break.
I call my mum when I have time.
Before opening my email, I check the list.
After lunch, I walk a little.
When I get home, I have a shower.
A plan with options: if this happens, we do that.
If it rains, we take the bus.
If the weather is good, we walk from the station.
If the train is late, I’ll let you know.
If I have time, I’ll call you later.
if it rains = si llueve (never «si lloverá»).
We take the bus if it rains.
We eat at a café if we find a free table.
Ana takes a bag if she buys big books.
Yes, I’ll go if I have time.
Yes, we leave at nine if you finish at eight.
Yes, I’ll help you if you wait for me a moment.
I’ll call you if I leave early.
In Argentina and Uruguay, people say “vos” instead of “tú”. Same meaning, different verb form.
With vos, the stress moves to the end of the verb.
Do you study Spanish on Tuesdays?
Do you read the newspaper in the morning?
Do you live near the centre?
You write a lot of messages.
Do you open the shop at nine?
Infinitive minus -r, plus -s, with an accent.
Vos uses te and tu, like tú.
Common forms to recognise: sos, tenés, querés, podés.
Don’t mix tú with vos verb forms.
Hi! You’re the new student, right?
And do you teach here, at the university?
You eat at home on Sundays.
You work a lot and study.
Nouns name people, places, things and ideas.
If it can take el/la/un/una, it is probably a noun.
Every noun is masculine or feminine, even objects.
Learn every noun with its article.
The day starts with a meeting.
The map is on the wall.
I have a problem with the computer.
The photo is in Laura’s hand.
Many words ending in -ma are masculine.
canción → canciones: the accent mark disappears.
Words that go with the noun change too.
el capital = money · la capital = capital city
Laura, what is in the box?
There are two books, three pencils and some photos.
There are three pencils in the box.
The photos are on the desk.
The room is small. The chairs are comfortable.
the new neighbourhood · the new house
the new neighbourhoods · the new houses
same form for masculine and feminine
a big hotel · a big house
a Spanish boy · a Spanish girl
a good book · a great city · very quiet
Look, Clara: this is the small room.
Articles go before the noun and agree with it.
Learn every noun with its article.
I see some friends on the terrace.
I see a café. The café is full.
Can you close the door? (the door of this room)
The sun is very strong today.
Where is the bathroom? (in this place)
She is a very creative teacher.
del = de + el · al = a + el
Sergio, where do we have the meeting?
Near the office there is a new café.
There is a free table on the terrace.
The café has a blue door.
I have the documents for the meeting.
Does the listener know which one?
Spanish has three distances: near me, near you, far from both.
That is a present for you.
esto never goes with a noun
este and ese are the most common.
this week · this year · in those days
Good morning. How much is this notebook?
I also need two small folders. And that folder?
Those boxes over there are big.
Where is it? Do you know what it is?
Possessives say who something belongs to.
mis = many things, not many owners
mine · yours · a friend of mine
Elena, do you see my keys? I can’t find them.
No. Are they in your backpack?
My keys are in my bag.
Our room is near the entrance.
The owner picks the word; the thing picks the form.
a bag of bread · a pack of napkins
I have lots of cups, but few plates.
There is a lot of fruit at the market.
There is enough coffee and enough chairs.
Luis, how many people are coming tomorrow?
I have many cups but few plates.
I buy two bottles of water.
All the shops close at six.
There is enough coffee in the kitchen.
Quantity words agree with the noun.
Subject pronouns say who does the action.
I cook; you wash the dishes. (contrast)
She gets up at seven and he at eight.
I live in Bogotá, and you in Lima.
get up · shower · wash · comb · get dressed · get ready · sit down · go to bed · stay
Diego goes to bed at twelve.
Lucía and Diego go to bed at eleven.
Other pronouns come in other lessons.
Diego, tomorrow I get up at seven.
I work at home and she works at the office.
We go to bed at eleven.
Here, there (near you), over there (far from both of us).
I am here, in the library.
Your backpack is there, next to your chair.
The Spanish books are over there, at the back.
My house is very far. The library is close.
Today I work at the library.
First I read my messages and then I study.
I can’t right now, I’m in class.
There is a lot of noise in the street.
There are a lot of people in the library today.
I have a lot of books at home.
Today I sleep badly: there is a lot of noise.
very + quality · a lot of + quantity
First I read and then I write.
The books are over there, at the back.
Ser: what is it? Estar: where is it / how is it now? Hay: what is there?
The office is on a quiet street.
There are two tables in the office.
The office is small and modern.
She is a designer → Es diseñadora.
My desk is next to the window.
Today the office is very tidy.
I am tired: I work a lot.
There is a bakery on the corner.
There are two cafés in front of the building.
There are a lot of free chairs in the room.
Is there water in the fridge?
es = what it is like · está = how it is now
There is a table next to the door.
The office is in the city centre.
There are two cafés on my street.
